claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Mg is initially uniformly distributed within the alloy matrix.
Exposure at 750–900 °C activates diffusion-driven phase separation in the alloy.
High-temperature exposure causes Mg to diffuse out of its supersaturated metastable solid-solution state.
Diffusing Mg segregates because doing so reduces the alloy's free energy.
Mg segregation promotes nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates preferentially form along grain boundaries and internal interfaces.
Thermally aged samples will contain distinct Mg-rich intermetallic phases relative to the initial uniform solid solution.
The size, distribution, and connectivity of Mg-rich intermetallic phases alter the formation and integrity of protective oxide layers.
Finely dispersed Mg-rich precipitates can preserve a protective oxide film and thereby retain corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Coarsened, continuous, or interconnected Mg-rich intermetallic networks act as weak links that compromise oxide-scale integrity.
Compromised oxide-scale integrity leads to accelerated corrosion and oxidation rates.
A critical temperature–aging-time combination exists at which Mg segregation becomes kinetically significant.
Below the proposed temperature–time threshold, the protective oxide layer is maintained.
Above the proposed temperature–time threshold, the protective oxide layer is disrupted.
Tens to hundreds of hours at 750–900 °C are sufficient to permit diffusion-driven phase separation.
